comments.author: @davidbrathwaite5779
comments.text:
What I find fascinating is that the thread snake was well known in Barbados for generations. I am in my late sixties and I remember my mother telling me about them in my childhood. Yet a scientist came and "discovered" them and named them like Columbus discovered America and the West Indies. Where I live in St. Philip, one of the driest parishes in the island with no forests, I have had three or four come into the house over a decade, so I expect that there are many more in the natural grass of the area. I think I can find pictures I took of two of them years ago. The idea that they live only in forested areas is a joke.

There is another very small Barbados snake that is far less common or is perhaps extinct. I saw one as a youngster. It was found in a neighbour's backyard in the housing area in St. Michael where I grew up. My friends and I put it in a bottle with grass and leaves, but it died in a few days likely from lack of food. It was somewhat thicker than a thread snake (like a juice box straw or the tube of a ballpoint pen) but of similar length with black and yellow bands.

comments.text: Simply making a video does not make something factual. Your explanation about Barbados is incomplete and misleading. Having no permanent rivers does not mean having no natural water systems. Barbados has natural gullies, underground water reserves, and systems for rainwater drainage. If your intention is to educate people, then present complete facts backed by proper research instead of spreading half-truths. Knowledge comes from research, not just making videos and presenting assumptions as facts
